name: Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)
analogy: Think of it as a desk of junior analysts who each write one short checklist. The first makes a rough call, and every analyst after that only studies the bars the desk has been getting wrong and writes a small correction. The final call is all the checklists added together.

steps.title: Start from a flat first guess
steps.description: Before it looks at any feature, the model makes the same guess for every bar: the average outcome in the training bars. Everything after this is a correction to that starting point.
steps.inExample: The training bars closed higher 6 bars later 51 percent of the time, so every bar starts at a 51 percent chance of closing higher.

steps.title: Measure where the guess is wrong
steps.description: For every training bar it compares the current guess with what actually happened. The gap is the error: large where the guess was badly off, near zero where it was already right.
steps.inExample: A bar that actually closed higher has an error of plus 49 points of probability; a bar that closed lower has an error of minus 51.

steps.title: Grow one small tree on the errors
steps.description: It builds a short decision tree, a few yes-or-no questions about the features, that sorts the bars into groups with similar errors. The tree is kept small on purpose so that it captures one simple pattern and nothing more.
steps.inExample: The first tree asks whether the relative strength index is under 30 and then whether volume is above its 20-bar average; bars answering yes to both were under-guessed.

steps.title: Add a small part of the correction
steps.description: The tree's correction is added to the running guess, but only a fraction of it. Taking small steps stops any single tree from dominating and makes the model harder to fool with noise.
steps.inExample: The oversold, high-volume group moves from a 51 percent to a 53 percent chance of closing higher; the rest barely move.

steps.title: Repeat a few hundred times
steps.description: Steps two to four run again and again. Each new tree looks only at what the trees before it still get wrong, so the model sharpens gradually. It stops when a held-back set of bars stops improving.
steps.inExample: After 300 trees the validation bars stop improving, so the model stops there and keeps those 300 trees.

steps.title: Score a new bar by adding up every tree
steps.description: A new bar is passed down every tree. Each tree contributes its small correction, the corrections are summed onto the starting guess, and the total is turned into a probability.
steps.inExample: The 14:35 bar collects small upward corrections from 190 trees and downward ones from 110, landing at a 58 percent chance of closing higher.

useFor.task: Direction calls from a table of features
useFor.example: Predicting whether MNQ's close 6 bars (30 minutes) after a 5-minute bar will be above that bar's close, from the 35 base features.
Finding out whether volume features or momentum features are doing the work, by reading how often and how usefully each feature is used in the trees.

useFor.task: A strong baseline before anything deeper
useFor.example: Running it on the same folds as a transformer so that the transformer has to beat a cheap, fast model to justify its training time.

useFor.task: Deciding whether to take another signal's trade
useFor.example: Taking only the breakout entries that the model scores above a 55 percent chance of reaching their target before their stop.

avoidWhen: The information is in the order of the bars themselves, such as the shape of the last 60 candles; a sequence model reads that directly, while this model only sees the summary features you hand it.
Prices will move far outside the range seen in training; trees cannot extend a trend beyond the values they were grown on.

example.scenario: A 5-minute MNQ bar closes at 14:35. The model was trained on the previous 12 months of bars and is asked whether the close 30 minutes later will be higher than this close.

input.summary: One row of features describing the bar that just closed, the same columns the model was trained on.

fields.name: close
fields.meaning: The price at which the 14:35 five-minute bar closed.

fields.name: relative strength index, 14 bars
fields.meaning: A momentum reading from 0 to 100; under 30 is commonly read as oversold.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading in this bar was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar, a measure of how much the market is moving.

fields.name: distance from the 50-bar moving average
fields.meaning: How far the close sits below its recent average price.

fields.name: return over the last 6 bars
fields.value: down about a third of a percent
fields.meaning: How much price has fallen over the previous 30 minutes.

output.summary: One probability for the bar, plus the features that pushed it there.

fields.name: probability the close is higher 6 bars later
fields.meaning: The summed vote of all 300 trees for this bar, against a 51 percent starting guess.

fields.name: call
fields.meaning: The side the probability falls on when the dividing line is 50 percent.

fields.name: largest push
fields.meaning: The feature whose trees added the most to this bar's probability.

example.reading: 58 percent is a modest lean, seven points above the starting guess. Whether it is worth a trade depends on costs: the lean has to be large enough that the average win covers commission and slippage, which is what the run page's net result measures.
